notes.h: Anatomical language, the vertebral column and the back
notes.body:
All descriptions assume the anatomical position: standing upright, facing forwards, arms by the sides with palms forward and feet together. The sagittal plane divides left from right (the median plane is the midline sagittal plane), the coronal plane divides front from back, and the transverse (axial) plane divides upper from lower.

- Medial/lateral: nearer to or further from the midline.
- Proximal/distal: nearer to or further from the root of a limb.
- Superficial/deep: nearer to or further from the surface.
- Movements: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, medial/lateral rotation, pronation/supination (forearm), inversion/eversion and dorsiflexion/plantarflexion (foot).

The vertebral column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and usually 4 coccygeal vertebrae. The thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary curvatures present at birth; the cervical and lumbar lordoses are secondary, appearing as the infant holds up its head and then walks. A typical vertebra has a body and a vertebral arch made of pedicles and laminae, which carries spinous, transverse and articular processes and encloses the vertebral foramen.

- Cervical: foramina in the transverse processes (the vertebral artery usually runs through C6 to C1), bifid spines from C3 to C6, C1 (atlas) has no body, C2 (axis) carries the dens, and C7 has a long palpable spine (vertebra prominens).
- Thoracic: costal facets for the ribs, heart-shaped bodies and long, downward-sloping spines.
- Lumbar: large kidney-shaped bodies and short, square spines.

Intervertebral discs combine an outer annulus fibrosus with a gel-like central nucleus pulposus, which is a notochord remnant. The anterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperextension; the posterior longitudinal ligament, ligamentum flavum, interspinous and supraspinous ligaments resist flexion. Extrinsic back muscles (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) move the upper limb. The intrinsic erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis, from lateral to medial) and the transversospinalis group are supplied by posterior rami.

Applied example: the adult spinal cord ends at about L1/L2 and the dural sac at S2, so lumbar puncture is done at L3/L4 or L4/L5. The line joining the iliac crests (the supracristal or Tuffier's line) crosses about L4. The needle passes skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid before reaching CSF.

Exam pitfalls:
- C1 to C7 nerves leave above the vertebra of the same number, C8 leaves below C7, and every nerve after that leaves below its own vertebra.
- A posterolateral lumbar disc prolapse usually compresses the traversing (lower) root, so an L4/L5 prolapse affects L5, not L4.

notes.h: Thorax: wall, pleura, lungs, mediastinum and heart
notes.body:
Ribs 1–7 are true ribs (their own costal cartilage reaches the sternum), ribs 8–12 are false ribs (they do not reach the sternum by their own cartilage), of which ribs 11–12 are floating. The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint) marks the second costal cartilage and lies level with the T4/T5 disc. That plane separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum and marks where the aortic arch begins and ends, where the trachea bifurcates and where the azygos vein drains into the superior vena cava.

Each intercostal space contains external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles. The neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above down) runs in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, between the internal and innermost layers. Chest drains therefore go in just above the upper border of the rib below, inside the 'triangle of safety' (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, fifth intercostal space).

- Parietal pleura has somatic nerves (intercostal and phrenic) and is sensitive to pain. Visceral pleura has only autonomic nerves.
- The lower lung border crosses ribs 6, 8 and 10 at the midclavicular, midaxillary and paravertebral lines. The pleura sits two ribs lower (8, 10, 12), leaving the costodiaphragmatic recess.
- The right lung has three lobes (horizontal and oblique fissures). The left has two lobes, a lingula and a cardiac notch.
- The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects usually go right.

The inferior mediastinum is divided into anterior, middle (heart and pericardium) and posterior parts. The posterior part holds the oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system and thoracic duct. The phrenic nerves (C3–C5) pass anterior to the lung roots and the vagi pass posterior. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum.

The right atrium forms the right heart border and the left ventricle most of the left border. The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface and the left atrium most of the base. The right coronary artery usually supplies the SA node and, in most people, the AV node. Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery, which is the right coronary in most people. The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior left ventricle and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.

Diaphragm openings: IVC at T8 (central tendon, with the right phrenic nerve), oesophagus at T10 (with the vagal trunks) and aorta at T12 (with the thoracic duct and often the azygos vein).

Applied example: a stab wound in the left fourth intercostal space beside the sternum enters the right ventricle first, because that chamber lies most anteriorly.

Exam pitfalls: placing the neurovascular bundle on the upper border of the rib, and confusing the lung and pleural reflection levels.

notes.h: Abdomen: wall, inguinal canal, gut supply and viscera
notes.body:
The transpyloric plane (L1) passes through the pylorus, the neck of the pancreas, the duodenojejunal flexure and the renal hila, and roughly marks the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.

Anterolateral wall layers: skin, fatty (Camper's) and membranous (Scarpa's) superficial fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and parietal peritoneum. Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass in front of rectus abdominis, so only transversalis fascia lies behind it.

The inguinal canal runs from the deep ring to the superficial ring. The deep ring lies at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the superficial ring lies above and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

- Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique.
- Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
- Roof: arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus. Floor: inguinal ligament.
- Contents: spermatic cord (or round ligament) and the ilioinguinal nerve.
- An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach's triangle medial to them. A femoral hernia appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Gut supply follows embryology. Foregut (coeliac trunk, T12) runs to the major duodenal papilla, midgut (superior mesenteric artery, L1) to the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the transverse colon, and hindgut (inferior mesenteric artery, L3) to the pectinate line. Visceral pain is referred to the epigastric, periumbilical and suprapubic regions respectively.

The epiploic foramen links the greater and lesser sacs. In front of it lies the hepatoduodenal ligament carrying the portal triad (bile duct to the right, hepatic artery to the left, portal vein behind both); behind it lies the IVC. Retroperitoneal structures include the kidneys, ureters, adrenals, aorta, IVC, duodenum (parts 2–4), pancreas (except the tail), and the ascending and descending colon.

- Portosystemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anorectum, umbilicus and retroperitoneum enlarge in portal hypertension, giving varices and caput medusae.
- Calot's triangle (cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior surface of the liver) usually contains the cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery.
- From front to back, the renal hilum holds vein, artery and pelvis. The left renal vein crosses between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery.

Applied example: early appendicitis causes vague periumbilical pain (visceral, midgut). The pain moves to McBurney's point, a third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

Exam pitfalls: confusing direct and indirect hernias, which are told apart by the inferior epigastric vessels and not by the scrotum; and forgetting that the duodenum is mostly retroperitoneal.

The bony pelvis is formed by the two hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis fused at the acetabulum), the sacrum and the coccyx. The pelvic inlet is bounded by the sacral promontory, the sacral alae, the arcuate and pectineal lines, the pubic crests and the pubic symphysis. Compared with the male pelvis, the typical female pelvis has a wider, more oval inlet, a wider subpubic angle, everted ischial spines and a larger outlet, all of which suit childbirth.
The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is formed by levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus) and coccygeus. It is supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and by branches of the pudendal nerve. Puborectalis loops around the anorectal junction, keeping the anorectal angle that helps maintain faecal continence.

The perineum is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind. The perineal body is a central fibromuscular anchor; a mediolateral episiotomy is cut to avoid extending into the anal sphincter.
- Pudendal nerve (S2–S4): leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, curves around the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen.
- Branches: inferior rectal (external anal sphincter, perianal skin), perineal and dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris. The ischial spine is the landmark for a pudendal block.
- Detrusor contraction is parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–S4); sympathetic fibres (T11–L2) relax the detrusor during filling.
- Erection is parasympathetic, emission sympathetic and ejaculation needs somatic contraction of bulbospongiosus via the pudendal nerve.

Male viscera: prostate cancers arise mainly in the peripheral zone, which can be felt on rectal examination. Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises in the transition zone around the urethra. The ductus deferens crosses above the ureter. Female viscera: the uterus is usually anteverted and anteflexed. The uterine artery crosses above the ureter beside the cervix ('water under the bridge'), so the ureter is at risk during hysterectomy. The ovarian vessels run in the suspensory ligament of the ovary. The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity when upright.

The pectinate line divides the anal canal into two parts:
- Above: endoderm, visceral nerves (painless), superior rectal vessels with portal drainage, internal iliac nodes, internal haemorrhoids.
- Below: ectoderm, somatic nerves (painful), inferior rectal vessels with systemic drainage, superficial inguinal nodes.

Exam pitfalls: testicular cancer spreads to para-aortic nodes because the testis descended from the posterior abdominal wall, whereas scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

notes.h: Upper limb: brachial plexus, nerve injuries and key regions
notes.body:
The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5–T1 and is organised into roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches. The roots pass between anterior and middle scalene, and the cords are named for their position around the axillary artery.

- Roots: dorsal scapular and long thoracic (C5–C7, serratus anterior). Upper trunk: suprascapular nerve.
- Lateral cord: musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.
- Medial cord: ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.
- Posterior cord: subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.

An Erb palsy (C5–C6), often from a traction birth injury or a fall that forces the head away from the shoulder, gives the 'waiter's tip' posture: arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated. A Klumpke palsy (C8–T1) follows forced arm abduction. It causes weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with clawing, and may cause Horner's syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres are damaged.

Peripheral nerve lesions:
- Axillary (surgical neck fracture, shoulder dislocation): weak deltoid, numb 'regimental badge' patch.
- Radial (midshaft humeral fracture in the radial groove): wrist drop, numbness over the dorsal first web space; triceps usually spared.
- Median at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome): thenar wasting, weak abductor pollicis brevis, numb palmar lateral three and a half digits. Sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
- Ulnar (at the elbow or wrist): clawing of the ring and little fingers, interosseous wasting and a positive Froment's sign. In the 'ulnar paradox', a wrist lesion claws more than an elbow lesion because the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is still working.
- Long thoracic: winging of the scapula.

The rotator cuff is supraspinatus (starts abduction, suprascapular nerve), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation, suprascapular and axillary nerves) and subscapularis (medial rotation, subscapular nerves). Deltoid continues abduction, and trapezius with serratus anterior rotates the scapula above 90°.

Regions: the cubital fossa contains, from lateral to medial, the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The carpal tunnel carries the median nerve and nine tendons (four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus). The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal. The anatomical snuffbox has the scaphoid in its floor and the radial artery crossing it.

Applied example: tenderness in the snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand suggests a scaphoid fracture. The blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole can undergo avascular necrosis.

Exam pitfalls: confusing a high median nerve lesion (forearm flexors also lost) with carpal tunnel syndrome, and forgetting which way the ulnar paradox runs.

notes.h: Lower limb: plexuses, regions, joints and nerve injuries
notes.body:
The lumbar plexus (L1–L4) gives the femoral nerve (quadriceps, knee jerk L3–L4), the obturator nerve (adductors) and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh. The sacral plexus (L4–S4) gives the sciatic nerve (L4–S3), the superior gluteal nerve (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae), the inferior gluteal nerve (gluteus maximus) and the pudendal nerve.

- Trendelenburg sign: with superior gluteal nerve palsy or weak hip abductors, the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side when the patient stands on the affected leg.
- Gluteal injections go in the upper outer quadrant or ventrogluteal site to avoid the sciatic nerve.

The femoral triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament, the medial border of sartorius and the medial border of adductor longus. From lateral to medial it contains the femoral nerve (outside the femoral sheath), femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal with its lymphatics. The femoral pulse lies at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

The popliteal fossa is bounded by biceps femoris, by semimembranosus and semitendinosus, and by the two heads of gastrocnemius. From superficial to deep it contains the tibial nerve, the popliteal vein and the popliteal artery. The common fibular nerve winds round the fibular neck and is easily damaged there, causing foot drop, weak eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot.

- Leg compartments: anterior (deep fibular nerve, dorsiflexion), lateral (superficial fibular nerve, eversion), posterior (tibial nerve, plantarflexion).
- Dermatomes: L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot and big toe, S1 lateral foot and heel. The ankle jerk tests S1–S2.

Knee: the anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur (Lachman test); the posterior cruciate stops it sliding backward. The medial meniscus is fixed to the medial collateral ligament, so is less mobile and more often torn. At the ankle, inversion injuries most often tear the anterior talofibular ligament.

Hip: the femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run up the neck inside the capsule. A displaced intracapsular neck fracture can tear them and cause avascular necrosis, which is why such fractures are often treated by arthroplasty rather than fixation. The leg is classically shortened and externally rotated.

Applied example: a patient who cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot and has numbness over its dorsum after a tight below-knee cast most likely has a common fibular nerve palsy at the fibular neck. An L5 radiculopathy is less likely if inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) is preserved.

Exam pitfall: the femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point) and the deep inguinal ring (midpoint of the inguinal ligament, from anterior superior iliac spine to pubic tubercle) use different landmarks.

notes.h: Head and neck: skull, cranial nerves, neck and larynx
notes.body:
Skull foramina and what passes through them:
- Cribriform plate: olfactory nerve (I). Optic canal: optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery.
- Superior orbital fissure: III, IV, V1 and VI, and the ophthalmic veins.
- Foramen rotundum: V2. Foramen ovale: V3. Foramen spinosum: middle meningeal artery.
- Internal acoustic meatus: VII and VIII. Jugular foramen: IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein. Hypoglossal canal: XII.

The pterion, where frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet, is thin and overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. A blow there can cause an extradural haematoma: a lucid interval followed by deterioration, with a biconvex (lens-shaped) clot on CT that does not cross suture lines. A subdural haematoma comes from torn bridging veins and is crescent-shaped.

Facial nerve: it leaves the stylomastoid foramen and divides inside the parotid into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches. A lower motor neuron lesion (e.g. Bell's palsy) weakens the whole of one side of the face. An upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke) spares the forehead because the upper face receives cortical input from both hemispheres.

Trigeminal nerve: V1 and V2 are sensory. V3 also supplies the muscles of mastication.

Tongue: general sensation to the anterior two-thirds comes through the lingual nerve (V3) and taste through the chorda tympani (VII). The posterior third is served by IX. All tongue muscles are supplied by XII except palatoglossus (X). With a lower motor neuron XII lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the weak side.

Neck: the anterior triangle is bounded by the midline, the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid and the mandible. The posterior triangle is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and the middle third of the clavicle. The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially and can be cut during lymph node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness and shoulder drooping. The carotid sheath contains the carotid artery (medially), internal jugular vein (laterally) and vagus nerve (behind, between them).
Larynx: the cricoid (C6) is the only complete cartilage ring. All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve). Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds. An emergency surgical airway goes through the cricothyroid membrane.

Applied example: after thyroidectomy, hoarseness suggests unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and stridor suggests bilateral injury. Loss of high pitch and voice fatigue suggest injury to the external laryngeal nerve, which runs with the superior thyroid artery.

Exam pitfalls: LR6 SO4 (lateral rectus by VI, superior oblique by IV, the rest by III), and remembering that a compressive third nerve palsy usually affects the pupil early.

notes.h: Embryology: early development and organ formation
notes.body:
Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (the future embryo) and an outer trophoblast, and implants from about day 6–7. Week 2 is the 'week of twos': a bilaminar disc (epiblast, hypoblast), two cavities (amniotic cavity, yolk sac) and two trophoblast layers.

In gastrulation (week 3), epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm. The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 27–28. Failure of closure gives anencephaly at the cranial end and spina bifida at the caudal end. Periconceptional folic acid reduces this risk.

- Ectoderm: epidermis, CNS and neural crest (ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, facial skeleton).
- Mesoderm: somites (sclerotome, myotome, dermatome), intermediate mesoderm (kidneys, gonads) and lateral plate (body wall, gut wall muscle, heart, vessels).
- Endoderm: gut and airway epithelium, liver, pancreas and thyroid follicular cells.

Weeks 3–8 (the embryonic period) are the time of greatest sensitivity to teratogens for major structural defects.

Fetal circulation: oxygenated placental blood in the umbilical vein bypasses the liver (ductus venosus) and crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium; right ventricular output mostly bypasses the lungs through the ductus arteriosus. After birth these become the ligamentum teres, ligamentum venosum, fossa ovalis and ligamentum arteriosum. In tetralogy of Fallot, forward and upward displacement of the outlet septum gives pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Pharyngeal apparatus:
- Arch 1 (V3): muscles of mastication, malleus and incus. Arch 2 (VII): muscles of facial expression, stapes, styloid process. Arch 3 (IX): stylopharyngeus. Arches 4 and 6 (X): pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles and the laryngeal cartilages.
- Pouch 1: middle ear and auditory tube. Pouch 2: palatine tonsil. Pouch 3: inferior parathyroids and thymus. Pouch 4: superior parathyroids.
- Arch arteries: 3rd, carotids; 4th, aortic arch (left) and proximal right subclavian; 6th, pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, which is why the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops lower.

Gut: the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord in week 6, rotates 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery and returns by week 10–12. Errors cause malrotation with volvulus. Omphalocele is a sac-covered persistence of the herniation; gastroschisis is a defect beside the umbilicus with no covering sac. Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct.

Exam pitfalls: the inferior parathyroids come from the third pouch (they migrate further than the superior ones), and a horseshoe kidney is caught under the inferior mesenteric artery as it ascends.

cards.f: Describe the anatomical position.
cards.b: Standing upright facing forwards, arms by the sides with palms facing forwards, feet together and pointing forwards. All directional terms refer to this position.

cards.f: Which plane divides the body into front and back parts?
cards.b: The coronal (frontal) plane. The sagittal plane divides left from right, and the transverse plane divides upper from lower.

cards.f: Which spinal curvatures are primary and which are secondary?
cards.b: The thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary (present in the fetus). The cervical lordosis develops as the infant holds up its head, and the lumbar lordosis as it starts to walk.

cards.f: Name three features that identify a cervical vertebra.
cards.b: Foramina in the transverse processes, a small body and, from C3 to C6, a bifid spinous process. C7 has a long non-bifid spine.

cards.f: Which nerve root does a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse usually compress?
cards.b: The L5 root, which passes down past the disc to leave below the L5 pedicle. A far-lateral prolapse can catch the exiting L4 root.

cards.f: At what level does the adult spinal cord end, and where is lumbar puncture performed?
cards.b: The conus medullaris ends at about L1/L2. Lumbar puncture is done at L3/L4 or L4/L5, below the cord, where the needle enters the lumbar cistern.

cards.f: List the layers a lumbar puncture needle passes through in the midline.
cards.b: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid, then the subarachnoid space.

cards.f: Which ligament of the spine resists hyperextension?
cards.b: The anterior longitudinal ligament, a broad band running down the front of the vertebral bodies and discs.

cards.f: What supplies the intrinsic (deep) back muscles, and how does this differ from the extrinsic group?
cards.b: Posterior rami of spinal nerves supply the intrinsic muscles such as erector spinae. The extrinsic muscles (e.g. trapezius, latissimus dorsi) are supplied by anterior rami or the accessory nerve, reflecting their limb origin.

cards.f: Name the three columns of erector spinae from lateral to medial.
cards.b: Iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis.

cards.f: What structures and events are associated with the sternal angle (T4/T5)?
cards.b: The second costal cartilage, the superior/inferior mediastinum boundary, the start and end of the aortic arch, the tracheal bifurcation and the azygos vein draining into the SVC.

cards.f: In what order do vessels and nerve lie in the costal groove?
cards.b: From top to bottom: vein, artery, nerve, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Needles therefore go in just above the upper border of the rib below.

cards.f: Give the boundaries of the 'triangle of safety' for chest drain insertion.
cards.b: Lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line level with the fifth intercostal space, with the apex below the axilla.

cards.f: Why does an inhaled foreign body usually lodge in the right lung?
cards.b: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

cards.f: At what vertebral levels do the IVC, oesophagus and aorta pass through the diaphragm?
cards.b: IVC at T8, oesophagus at T10 and aorta at T12 (the aorta actually passes behind the median arcuate ligament).

cards.f: Which chamber forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart?
cards.b: The right ventricle. The left atrium forms most of the base (posterior surface).

cards.f: How is coronary dominance defined?
cards.b: By which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery. In most people this is the right coronary artery.

cards.f: Where do the lung borders and pleural reflections lie at the midclavicular, midaxillary and paravertebral lines?
cards.b: Lungs: ribs 6, 8 and 10. Pleura: ribs 8, 10 and 12. The gap between them is the costodiaphragmatic recess.

cards.f: Why can left atrial enlargement cause hoarseness?
cards.b: An enlarged left atrium or pulmonary artery can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve where it hooks under the aortic arch (Ortner's syndrome), weakening the left vocal fold.

cards.f: Why is diaphragmatic pleural irritation felt at the shoulder tip?
cards.b: The central diaphragmatic pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), and C4 also supplies the skin over the shoulder, so the pain is referred there.

cards.f: Name the structures at the transpyloric plane (L1).
cards.b: The pylorus, neck of the pancreas, duodenojejunal flexure, renal hila, fundus of the gallbladder, and roughly the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.

cards.f: Give the walls of the inguinal canal.
cards.b: Anterior: external oblique aponeurosis (plus internal oblique laterally). Posterior: transversalis fascia (plus conjoint tendon medially). Roof: arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus. Floor: inguinal ligament.

cards.f: How do you tell a direct inguinal hernia from an indirect one anatomically?
cards.b: An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle medial to them.

cards.f: Name the boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle.
cards.b: The inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the lateral border of rectus abdominis medially and the inguinal ligament inferiorly.

cards.f: Which arteries supply the foregut, midgut and hindgut, and from which levels do they arise?
cards.b: Coeliac trunk (T12), superior mesenteric artery (L1) and inferior mesenteric artery (L3).

cards.f: Where is visceral pain from the foregut, midgut and hindgut referred?
cards.b: Epigastrium, periumbilical region and suprapubic region respectively.

cards.f: List the boundaries of Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle and its key content.
cards.b: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. It usually contains the cystic artery.

cards.f: Name the four main sites of portosystemic anastomosis.
cards.b: Lower oesophagus (left gastric with oesophageal veins), anorectum (superior with middle and inferior rectal veins), umbilicus (paraumbilical with epigastric veins) and retroperitoneum.

cards.f: In what order do structures lie in the renal hilum from front to back?
cards.b: Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.

cards.f: What is the nutcracker phenomenon?
cards.b: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. It can cause haematuria, flank pain or a left varicocele.

cards.f: Name the parts of levator ani and state its main nerve supply.
cards.b: Puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus. It is supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve.

cards.f: Describe the course of the pudendal nerve.
cards.b: It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, curves around the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine, and runs through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.

cards.f: What landmark guides a pudendal nerve block?
cards.b: The ischial spine, felt through the vaginal wall. The nerve passes just behind it with the sacrospinous ligament.

cards.f: Why is the ureter at risk during hysterectomy?
cards.b: It passes under the uterine artery about 1–2 cm lateral to the cervix ('water under the bridge'), so it can be clamped or tied with the artery.

cards.f: Contrast the anal canal above and below the pectinate line.
cards.b: Above: endoderm, visceral nerves (painless), portal venous drainage, internal iliac nodes. Below: ectoderm, somatic nerves (painful), systemic venous drainage, superficial inguinal nodes.

cards.f: In which zone of the prostate do most adenocarcinomas arise, and why does it matter?
cards.b: The peripheral zone, which lies against the rectum and so can be felt on digital rectal examination.

cards.f: Which autonomic outflow drives bladder emptying?
cards.b: Parasympathetic fibres in the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) contract the detrusor. Sympathetic fibres (T11–L2) relax it during filling.

cards.f: Where does testicular cancer first spread to via lymph, and why?
cards.b: The para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near L1–L2, because the testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and keeps its lymph drainage when it descends.

cards.f: What is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in an upright woman?
cards.b: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas), where blood or pus may collect. It can be reached through the posterior vaginal fornix.

cards.f: Give two pelvic features typical of the female pelvis compared with the male.
cards.b: A wider subpubic angle and a wider, more oval inlet. A larger outlet and everted ischial spines are also typical.

cards.f: From which anterior rami does the brachial plexus arise?
cards.b: C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.

cards.f: Which cord gives the ulnar nerve, and which gives the radial and axillary nerves?
cards.b: The ulnar nerve comes from the medial cord. The radial and axillary nerves come from the posterior cord.

cards.f: Describe the posture of an Erb palsy and the roots involved.
cards.b: C5–C6 injury: arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated ('waiter's tip').

cards.f: What nerve is at risk with a midshaft humeral fracture, and what is the main sign?
cards.b: The radial nerve in the radial groove. It causes wrist drop; triceps is usually spared because its branches leave higher up.

cards.f: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
cards.b: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves before the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

cards.f: What is the ulnar paradox?
cards.b: A distal (wrist) ulnar lesion causes more obvious clawing than a proximal (elbow) lesion, because the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus still flexes the fingers.

cards.f: Name the rotator cuff muscles and their nerve supply.
cards.b: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve), teres minor (axillary nerve) and subscapularis (upper and lower subscapular nerves).

cards.f: What passes through the carpal tunnel?
cards.b: The median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus.

cards.f: Give the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial.
cards.b: Biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The radial nerve lies just lateral, under brachioradialis.

cards.f: Why is the proximal pole of the scaphoid at risk of avascular necrosis?
cards.b: Its blood supply enters distally from branches of the radial artery and runs back towards the proximal pole, so a waist fracture can cut it off.

cards.f: Which nerve injury causes winging of the scapula?
cards.b: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), which supplies serratus anterior. It may be damaged during axillary surgery.

cards.f: Give the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial.
cards.b: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal (lymphatics). The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

cards.f: Where is the femoral pulse felt?
cards.b: At the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

cards.f: Explain a positive Trendelenburg sign.
cards.b: When standing on the affected leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite side because the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus, superior gluteal nerve) on the stance side are weak.

cards.f: Which nerve is injured by a fibular neck fracture, and what deficits result?
cards.b: The common fibular nerve: foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion), weak eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.

cards.f: Name the order of structures behind the medial malleolus.
cards.b: From front to back: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery and veins, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.

cards.f: Why do displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis?
cards.b: The retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery run up the neck inside the capsule and are torn, cutting off the head's main blood supply.

cards.f: Which knee ligament stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur, and how is it tested?
cards.b: The anterior cruciate ligament, tested with the Lachman test (most sensitive) and the anterior drawer test.

cards.f: Which ankle ligament is most often injured in an inversion sprain?
cards.b: The anterior talofibular ligament, part of the lateral collateral complex.

cards.f: Which nerve roots does the knee jerk test, and which does the ankle jerk test?
cards.b: Knee jerk: L3–L4 (femoral nerve). Ankle jerk: S1–S2 (tibial nerve).

cards.f: How can you tell an L5 radiculopathy from a common fibular nerve palsy?
cards.b: Both cause foot drop. In L5 radiculopathy, inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) and hip abduction are also weak; in fibular palsy they are spared.

cards.f: What causes meralgia paraesthetica?
cards.b: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, usually near the anterior superior iliac spine under the inguinal ligament. It causes burning numbness of the lateral thigh with no weakness.

cards.f: What passes through the jugular foramen?
cards.b: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI and the internal jugular vein (from the sigmoid sinus and inferior petrosal sinus).

cards.f: Why is the pterion clinically important?
cards.b: The bone there is thin and overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. A fracture can tear the artery and cause an extradural haematoma.

cards.f: How do extradural and subdural haematomas differ on CT?
cards.b: Extradural: biconvex (lens-shaped) and limited by sutures, usually arterial. Subdural: crescent-shaped, crosses sutures, from torn bridging veins.

cards.f: Why does an upper motor neuron facial palsy spare the forehead?
cards.b: The motor neurons for the upper face receive input from both hemispheres, so one-sided cortical damage leaves forehead movement intact.

cards.f: Give the nerve supply of the tongue.
cards.b: Anterior two-thirds: general sensation by the lingual nerve (V3), taste by the chorda tympani (VII). Posterior third: IX for both. Muscles: XII, except palatoglossus (X).

cards.f: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal folds?
cards.b: Posterior cricoarytenoid, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

cards.f: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
cards.b: Cricothyroid, supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It tenses the vocal folds.

cards.f: What are the contents of the carotid sheath?
cards.b: The common then internal carotid artery (medial), internal jugular vein (lateral) and vagus nerve (between them, behind). The deep cervical nodes lie along it.

cards.f: Which nerve is at risk during lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle, and what is the result?
cards.b: The accessory nerve (XI), which runs superficially across the triangle. Injury weakens trapezius, causing shoulder droop and difficulty abducting above 90°.

cards.f: Give the nerve supply of the extraocular muscles.
cards.b: LR6 SO4: lateral rectus by VI, superior oblique by IV. The rest (superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique) and levator palpebrae superioris by III.

cards.f: Why is a 'surgical' third nerve palsy usually pupil-involving?
cards.b: Parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so external compression (e.g. posterior communicating artery aneurysm) affects them early. Ischaemic (diabetic) palsies often spare the pupil.

cards.f: What happens during week 2 of development ('week of twos')?
cards.b: The bilaminar disc (epiblast and hypoblast) forms, two cavities appear (amniotic cavity and yolk sac), and the trophoblast splits into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.

cards.f: What is gastrulation, and when does it occur?
cards.b: In week 3, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm.

cards.f: Name four derivatives of neural crest cells.
cards.b: Dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, and much of the facial skeleton and connective tissue.

cards.f: When do the neuropores close, and what defects follow failure of closure?
cards.b: Cranial neuropore about day 25 (failure gives anencephaly) and caudal neuropore about day 27–28 (failure gives spina bifida).

cards.f: What do the three parts of a somite form?
cards.b: Sclerotome: vertebrae and ribs. Myotome: skeletal muscle. Dermatome: dermis of the back.

cards.f: Name the adult remnants of the ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus and umbilical vein.
cards.b: Ligamentum arteriosum, ligamentum venosum and ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver).

cards.f: List the four features of tetralogy of Fallot and the underlying defect.
cards.b: Pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy, caused by forward and upward displacement of the outlet (infundibular) septum.

cards.f: What do the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches form?
cards.b: Third: inferior parathyroids and thymus. Fourth: superior parathyroids (and the ultimopharyngeal body, which gives the parafollicular C cells).

cards.f: Which pharyngeal arch gives the muscles of facial expression and what nerve supplies it?
cards.b: The second arch, supplied by the facial nerve (VII). It also gives the stapes and styloid process.

cards.f: Distinguish omphalocele from gastroschisis.
cards.b: Omphalocele: midline gut herniation through the umbilicus covered by a membrane sac, often with other anomalies. Gastroschisis: a defect usually right of the umbilicus with no sac, so the bowel is exposed.

cards.f: Why does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop lower than the right?
cards.b: On the left it hooks under the ductus arteriosus (6th arch) and the aortic arch. On the right the distal 6th and 5th arch arteries disappear, so it hooks around the subclavian artery (4th arch).

cards.f: Describe midgut rotation.
cards.b: The midgut herniates into the cord in week 6, rotates a total of 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery axis and returns by weeks 10–12.

questions.q: Which movement takes a body part away from the median plane?
questions.why: Abduction moves a part away from the midline; adduction brings it back towards the midline.

questions.q: A posterolateral disc prolapse at L5/S1 most often compresses which nerve root?
questions.why: A posterolateral prolapse catches the traversing root, which at L5/S1 is S1. The exiting L5 root passes above the disc in the foramen.

questions.q: Through which opening in the diaphragm does the oesophagus pass, and at what level?
questions.why: The oesophagus passes through the oesophageal hiatus in the right crus at T10, with the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

questions.q: In a right-dominant coronary circulation, which artery most commonly supplies the AV node?
questions.why: The AV nodal artery usually arises from the dominant artery at the crux, which in a right-dominant heart is the right coronary artery.

questions.q: During a hernia repair, a sac is seen emerging medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
questions.why: A direct inguinal hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. An indirect hernia emerges lateral to them through the deep ring.

questions.q: Internal haemorrhoids are typically painless. What is the best anatomical explanation?
options: They are drained by systemic veins
They lie above the pectinate line, where the mucosa has visceral nerves
They are supplied by the inferior rectal nerve
They are lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium
questions.why: Above the pectinate line the anal canal comes from endoderm and has visceral nerves that are not sensitive to cutting or pricking pain.

questions.q: A man has a midshaft fracture of the humerus. Which deficit is most likely?
options: Inability to abduct the arm beyond 15°
Wrist drop with numbness over the dorsal first web space
Clawing of the ring and little fingers
questions.why: The radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the back of the humeral shaft. Injury there paralyses the wrist and finger extensors.

questions.q: Which muscles are paralysed in a superior gluteal nerve injury?
options: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae
questions.why: The superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae, the main hip abductors and stabilisers.

questions.q: Which structure passes through the foramen ovale?
questions.why: V3 passes through the foramen ovale. V2 goes through the foramen rotundum and the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum.

questions.q: A patient asked to protrude her tongue finds it deviates to the left, with left-sided wasting and fasciculation. Where is the lesion?
questions.why: Wasting and fasciculation point to a lower motor neuron lesion. The intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue towards the weak left side.

questions.q: Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands?
questions.why: The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroids and the thymus. They migrate down with the thymus and end up below the superior parathyroids from pouch 4.

questions.q: Explain why lumbar puncture is performed at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace, and name the surface landmark used to find this level.
markScheme: The adult spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at about L1/L2.
The dural sac (and subarachnoid space) continues to about S2, forming the lumbar cistern.
Below the cord, the needle meets floating cauda equina roots that move aside, so cord injury is avoided.
The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests (Tuffier's or supracristal line) crosses about L4.
questions.modelAnswer: The adult spinal cord ends at roughly L1/L2, but the dura and arachnoid continue down to about S2, forming the CSF-filled lumbar cistern. A needle at L3/L4 or L4/L5 enters this cistern below the cord. The cauda equina roots float in CSF and tend to move away from the needle, so the procedure is much safer than at higher levels. The level is found by drawing a line between the highest points of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line), which usually crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/L5 space.

questions.q: A chest drain is needed for a pneumothorax. State where it should be inserted and explain the anatomical reasons.
markScheme: Inside the triangle of safety: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, line level with the fifth intercostal space.
Enter just above the upper border of the rib below.
The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above.
Staying at or above the fifth space and in the midaxillary region avoids the diaphragm, liver/spleen and the long thoracic nerve and vessels.
questions.modelAnswer: The drain goes in the triangle of safety, bounded by the lateral edge of pectoralis major, the anterior edge of latissimus dorsi and a line level with the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla. The needle and drain should pass just above the upper border of the rib below, because the intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under the rib above. Staying in this triangle avoids the internal thoracic vessels in front and the long thoracic nerve and thoracodorsal bundle behind. Keeping at or above the fifth space reduces the risk of puncturing the diaphragm and the liver or spleen.

questions.q: Explain why the pain of early appendicitis starts around the umbilicus and later moves to the right iliac fossa.
markScheme: The appendix is midgut, and its visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres to about the T10 segment.
Visceral pain is poorly localised and referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus.
When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum (somatic nerves), pain is sharply localised over the appendix (McBurney's point).
questions.modelAnswer: The appendix is part of the midgut. Its visceral afferent fibres travel with the sympathetic nerves and enter the cord at about T10. Visceral pain is vague and is referred to the dermatome of that segment, which lies around the umbilicus. As the inflammation spreads to the overlying parietal peritoneum, which has somatic nerves from the lower intercostal and L1 segments, the pain becomes sharp and well localised over the appendix, typically at McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the testis and of the scrotal skin, and explain the clinical significance.
markScheme: The testis drains to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at about L1–L2.
This is because the testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and its lymphatics (with the testicular vessels) are drawn down as it descends.
Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
So testicular tumours spread to para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes, and inguinal lymphadenopathy points to scrotal or other perineal disease.
questions.modelAnswer: The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys and descends through the inguinal canal, taking its vessels and lymphatics with it. Its lymph therefore drains back to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near the origin of the gonadal arteries, around L1–L2. The scrotal skin, by contrast, is ordinary perineal skin and drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. In practice, testicular cancer spreads first to retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes, which are staged with CT. Enlarged inguinal nodes suggest scrotal skin, penile or anal pathology instead. This is one reason orchidectomy for suspected cancer uses an inguinal rather than a scrotal approach.

questions.q: Compare the clinical features of a median nerve lesion at the wrist with one at the elbow.
markScheme: Both: weakness of the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), thenar wasting, lateral two lumbricals weak.
Both: sensory loss over the palmar lateral three and a half digits.
Wrist lesion: sensation over the thenar eminence preserved (palmar cutaneous branch leaves proximally).
Elbow lesion: also loss of pronation and forearm flexors (FDS, lateral FDP, FPL), so a 'hand of benediction' appears when making a fist.
Elbow lesion: thenar eminence sensation is also lost.
questions.modelAnswer: A lesion at either level weakens abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis, causing thenar wasting. The lateral two lumbricals are also weak, and sensation is lost over the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits. At the wrist the palmar cutaneous branch has already left, so thenar sensation is kept. A lesion at the elbow also paralyses pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus. Pronation is weak, the index and middle fingers stay extended when the patient tries to make a fist (hand of benediction), and thenar sensation is lost.

questions.q: List the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial and state one clinical use of this arrangement.
markScheme: Femoral nerve (outside the femoral sheath).
Femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymphatics, deep inguinal node) — in that order medially.
Clinical use: the artery is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, so femoral venous access is just medial to the pulse (or nerve block just lateral).
questions.modelAnswer: From lateral to medial the femoral triangle contains the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, the femoral vein and the femoral canal, which carries lymphatics and often a deep inguinal node (the mnemonic NAVY). The artery, vein and canal sit inside the femoral sheath; the nerve lies outside it. Clinically, the femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point. The femoral vein can then be cannulated just medial to the pulse, and a femoral nerve block placed just lateral to it.

questions.q: State the boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck and name two important contents.
markScheme: Anterior boundary: posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
Posterior boundary: anterior border of trapezius.
Base (inferior): middle third of the clavicle.
Any two contents: accessory nerve (XI), external jugular vein, trunks of the brachial plexus, subclavian artery (third part), cervical plexus cutaneous branches, occipital and supraclavicular nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior triangle lies between the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid in front, the anterior border of trapezius behind and the middle third of the clavicle below. Its roof is the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and its floor is muscle covered by prevertebral fascia. Important contents include the accessory nerve, which crosses the triangle superficially and is vulnerable in node biopsies. Others include the external jugular vein, the trunks of the brachial plexus, the third part of the subclavian artery and the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.

questions.q: Describe the three shunts in fetal circulation and what each becomes after birth.
markScheme: Ductus venosus: carries umbilical venous blood past the liver to the IVC; becomes the ligamentum venosum.
Foramen ovale: right-to-left atrial shunt; closes functionally at birth as left atrial pressure rises, leaving the fossa ovalis.
Ductus arteriosus: pulmonary trunk to aorta, bypassing the lungs; becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
Closure is triggered by lung expansion (falling pulmonary resistance), loss of the placenta and rising oxygen tension with falling prostaglandin levels.
questions.modelAnswer: The ductus venosus carries much of the oxygenated umbilical venous blood past the liver into the IVC; after birth it becomes the ligamentum venosum. The foramen ovale lets blood from the IVC cross from the right to the left atrium. When the lungs expand at birth, pulmonary resistance falls and left atrial pressure rises above right, pressing the valve shut and leaving the fossa ovalis. The ductus arteriosus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the high-resistance fetal lungs. Rising oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin levels make it constrict, and it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.q: Explain the 'ulnar paradox' and use it to predict the hand posture after an ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow compared with one at the wrist.
markScheme: Ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, interossei and hypothenar muscles.
Loss of the lumbricals and interossei leaves extension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints of the ring and little fingers (claw).
Flexion at the IP joints depends on flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers, supplied by the ulnar nerve in the forearm.
In a wrist lesion FDP is intact, so IP flexion is strong and clawing is marked.
In an elbow lesion FDP (ulnar half) is also paralysed, so the fingers are less flexed and clawing is milder.
The paradox: the more proximal lesion has more motor loss but less deformity.
questions.modelAnswer: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, all interossei and the medial two lumbricals. These muscles flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints. When they are lost, the long extensors pull the ring and little fingers into MCP extension. Flexor digitorum profundus, if it still works, then flexes the IP joints, producing a claw. In a wrist lesion the ulnar half of FDP, supplied in the forearm, is intact, so clawing is marked. In an elbow lesion FDP to these fingers is also paralysed, so the IP joints are not pulled into flexion and the claw is milder, even though more muscles are weak.

questions.q: Explain why a lesion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve may be the presenting sign of a thoracic tumour, but a right-sided lesion is less likely to be.
markScheme: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch next to the ligamentum arteriosum, deep in the thorax.
It is therefore exposed to tumours of the left lung hilum, aortopulmonary window nodes and aortic aneurysms.
The right nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck and does not enter the mediastinum to the same extent.
This asymmetry stems from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arch arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus in the thorax and loops under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, in the aortopulmonary window. Lung cancers of the left hilum, enlarged mediastinal nodes and aortic arch aneurysms can compress it, causing hoarseness from a paralysed left vocal fold, sometimes before other symptoms appear. The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery at the root of the neck, so mediastinal disease rarely reaches it. The difference is developmental. On the left the nerve is caught under the sixth arch artery, whose remnant is the ductus arteriosus. On the right the distal sixth arch artery regresses, so the nerve moves up to the fourth arch derivative, the subclavian.

questions.q:
Mr Daniel Okafor, a 42-year-old warehouse worker, felt sudden low back pain while lifting a heavy box. Over the next day the pain spread down the back of his left thigh and into the outer side of his foot. On examination, straight leg raising on the left produces pain at 35°. Plantarflexion of the left foot is weak, with difficulty standing on tiptoe on that side. The left ankle jerk is absent, the knee jerks are normal, and there is reduced pinprick sensation over the lateral border of the left foot and the sole. Perianal sensation and bladder function are normal.

Identify the most likely level and nerve root involved, explain the anatomy that produces each finding, and outline the red-flag features that would change management.
markScheme: Most likely posterolateral disc prolapse at L5/S1 compressing the S1 root.
Posterolateral prolapse affects the traversing root (S1 at L5/S1) because the exiting L5 root lies above the disc in the foramen.
Pain in the posterior thigh and lateral foot follows the S1 dermatome and the course of the sciatic nerve.
Weak plantarflexion: gastrocnemius and soleus are mainly S1–S2 via the tibial nerve.
Absent ankle jerk: S1 reflex arc (tibial nerve).
Sensory loss on the lateral foot and sole matches the S1 dermatome.
Positive straight leg raise: stretches L5/S1 roots through the sciatic nerve; tension on an inflamed root causes pain.
Normal knee jerk excludes L3–L4 involvement.
Disc anatomy: the annulus fibrosus is weakest posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow.
Red flags of cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, bilateral symptoms, sexual dysfunction — need emergency MRI and surgical referral.
Other red flags: progressive motor deficit, fever, weight loss, history of cancer, trauma.
questions.modelAnswer:
The picture fits a posterolateral prolapse of the L5/S1 disc compressing the left S1 nerve root. The annulus fibrosus is thinnest posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow, so the nucleus pulposus tends to herniate there. At L5/S1 the exiting L5 root has already passed above the disc in the upper part of the foramen. A posterolateral bulge therefore catches the traversing S1 root as it heads for the S1 foramen.

Each finding maps onto S1:
- Pain radiating down the back of the thigh to the outer foot follows the course of the sciatic nerve and the S1 dermatome.
- Weak plantarflexion and difficulty rising on tiptoe reflect gastrocnemius and soleus, supplied mainly by S1–S2 through the tibial nerve.
- The absent ankle jerk shows interruption of the S1 reflex arc. The normal knee jerk shows that L3–L4 are intact.
- Reduced sensation on the lateral border and sole of the foot matches the S1 dermatome. An L5 lesion would affect the dorsum and great toe and weaken dorsiflexion of the great toe.
- A positive straight leg raise at a low angle means that stretching the sciatic nerve pulls on an inflamed, tethered root.

Red flags change management. Cauda equina syndrome is suggested by saddle or perianal numbness, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, sexual dysfunction or symptoms in both legs. It needs emergency MRI and urgent surgical decompression. Progressive or severe motor weakness also warrants urgent imaging. Fever, weight loss, a history of cancer, immunosuppression or significant trauma raise the possibility of infection, malignancy or fracture. Without red flags, most disc prolapses settle with analgesia, staying active and physiotherapy, and imaging is reserved for persistent or worsening symptoms.

questions.q:
Mrs Helen Price, 68, is brought to the emergency department with crushing central chest pain. Her ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, and she has sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 44/min, which later progresses to complete heart block. Coronary angiography confirms an occluded artery, and the left anterior descending artery is patent. She is right-coronary dominant.

Using coronary anatomy, explain which artery is most likely occluded, which territories are at risk, and why she developed bradycardia and heart block. Explain how the findings would differ if she were left dominant, and discuss why infarction of this territory may also involve the right ventricle.
markScheme: Leads II, III and aVF reflect the inferior wall of the left ventricle.
In right dominance the right coronary artery gives the posterior interventricular artery, so the RCA is the likely culprit.
RCA territories: right atrium, most of the right ventricle, inferior LV wall, posterior third of the septum.
SA nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 60% of people: ischaemia causes sinus bradycardia.
AV nodal artery arises from the dominant artery at the crux (RCA here): AV block.
Inferior MI heart block is often due to AV nodal ischaemia and increased vagal tone, and is often temporary.
In left dominance the circumflex gives the posterior interventricular and AV nodal arteries, so inferior MI may come from circumflex occlusion.
Proximal RCA occlusion before the acute marginal branches causes right ventricular infarction.
RV infarction: hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs; right-sided leads (V4R) show ST elevation.
Clinical relevance: RV infarction is preload-dependent, so nitrates and diuretics can worsen hypotension.
LAD patent excludes anterior/septal territory as primary.
Clear, structured explanation linking anatomy to physiology.
questions.modelAnswer:
Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the left ventricle. In a right-dominant circulation, the right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove to the crux and gives off the posterior interventricular artery. That artery supplies the inferior LV wall and the posterior third of the septum. With the LAD patent, the right coronary artery is the most likely culprit.

The RCA supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, the inferior left ventricle and the posterior septum. Its conduction branches explain the arrhythmias. In roughly six people out of ten the SA nodal artery comes from the proximal RCA, so ischaemia slows the sinus rate. The AV nodal artery arises from the dominant artery at the crux, which here is the RCA, so AV nodal ischaemia causes progressive heart block. The inferior wall also has many vagal afferents, and the reflex increase in vagal tone (the Bezold–Jarisch reflex) adds to the bradycardia. AV block after inferior infarction often resolves as nodal perfusion and vagal tone recover, although some patients need temporary pacing.

In a left-dominant heart the circumflex continues to the crux, giving off the posterior interventricular and AV nodal arteries. An inferior infarct with heart block could then come from circumflex occlusion. It would often extend into the lateral wall, with changes in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, and might cause a larger loss of left ventricular muscle.

If the RCA is blocked before its acute marginal branches, the right ventricular free wall also infarcts. Typical signs are hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and clear lung fields, and right-sided chest leads (especially V4R) show ST elevation. The damaged right ventricle depends on adequate filling, so venodilators such as nitrates, or diuretics, can cause severe hypotension. Fluids and urgent reperfusion are central to treatment.

questions.q:
Mr Tomasz Nowak, 55, has a long history of alcohol excess and has drunk more than a bottle of spirits a day for many years. He is brought to the emergency department after vomiting a large amount of fresh red blood at home. He is pale, his pulse is 112/min and his blood pressure is 98/60 mmHg. On examination he has spider naevi, a distended abdomen with shifting dullness, dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus and a firm, shrunken liver edge. His platelet count is low and the spleen is palpable.

Explain the anatomy of the hepatic portal system and the sites of portosystemic anastomosis. Use this to account for his haematemesis, the periumbilical veins and the splenomegaly.
markScheme: Portal vein formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins (inferior mesenteric usually joins splenic).
Portal vein carries about 75% of hepatic blood flow; runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament behind bile duct and hepatic artery.
Cirrhosis raises intrahepatic resistance, so portal pressure rises (portal hypertension).
Blood is diverted through portosystemic anastomoses, which dilate.
Lower oesophagus: left gastric (portal) and oesophageal tributaries of azygos (systemic) — varices that can rupture, causing haematemesis.
Umbilicus: paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament reopen and connect with superficial epigastric veins — caput medusae.
Anorectum: superior rectal (portal) with middle/inferior rectal (systemic) — rectal varices.
Retroperitoneum: colic veins with lumbar/renal veins.
Splenic vein congestion causes splenomegaly; hypersplenism causes thrombocytopenia.
Ascites from portal hypertension plus low albumin.
questions.modelAnswer:
The hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas, where the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein. It runs up in the free edge of the lesser omentum (the hepatoduodenal ligament), behind the bile duct and hepatic artery, and supplies about three-quarters of the liver's blood flow. Portal blood crosses the hepatic sinusoids and leaves through the hepatic veins into the IVC.

In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerating nodules raise resistance to flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension. Blood takes alternative routes through connections between portal and systemic veins, which dilate under the raised pressure:
- Lower oesophagus: the left gastric vein (portal) connects with oesophageal veins draining to the azygos system (systemic). The dilated submucosal varices have thin walls and can rupture, giving large haematemeses like Mr Nowak's.
- Umbilicus: paraumbilical veins running in the falciform ligament with the ligamentum teres reopen and drain into the superficial epigastric veins of the abdominal wall. This produces veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae).
- Anorectum: the superior rectal vein (portal) connects with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic), giving anorectal varices, which are distinct from ordinary haemorrhoids.
- Retroperitoneum: colic and other bowel veins connect with lumbar, renal and phrenic veins.

The splenic vein drains into the high-pressure portal system, so the spleen becomes congested and enlarges. An enlarged spleen traps and destroys platelets (hypersplenism), explaining the low platelet count, which also makes bleeding worse. Ascites results from raised sinusoidal pressure combined with the low albumin of liver failure and sodium retention. Spider naevi reflect oestrogen excess because the liver fails to clear it.

questions.q:
Ms Aisha Rahman, 34, is in labour with her first baby, who weighs 4.1 kg at birth. The second stage lasts over three hours and the head is in an occipito-posterior position. A pudendal nerve block is given, a mediolateral episiotomy is performed and the baby is delivered with forceps. The perineum is repaired and no anal sphincter tear is recognised at the time. Six weeks later, at her postnatal check, she reports occasional faecal urgency and leakage of flatus that she finds embarrassing.

Describe the anatomy of the pelvic floor and perineum relevant to her delivery. Explain the course of the pudendal nerve and the landmark for the block, why a mediolateral rather than a midline episiotomy is preferred, and the anatomical mechanisms that maintain faecal continence and how childbirth may disrupt them.
markScheme: Pelvic diaphragm: levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus.
Perineum divided by the line between ischial tuberosities into urogenital and anal triangles.
Perineal body: central fibromuscular point where bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter and levator fibres meet.
Pudendal nerve S2–S4: exits greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, around sacrospinous ligament/ischial spine, enters lesser sciatic foramen, runs in pudendal canal.
Block landmark: ischial spine palpated transvaginally; anaesthetises most of the perineum.
Mediolateral episiotomy directed away from the midline reduces the risk of extension into the external anal sphincter and rectum.
Continence: internal anal sphincter (smooth, sympathetic, resting tone), external anal sphincter (skeletal, inferior rectal nerve), puborectalis sling keeping the anorectal angle.
Also rectal compliance and anal mucosal sensation (below pectinate line, somatic).
Childbirth can tear the sphincters (obstetric anal sphincter injury) and stretch or compress the pudendal nerve, especially with prolonged second stage and forceps.
Symptoms of urgency and flatus leakage suggest external sphincter weakness; endoanal ultrasound assesses sphincter defects.
Well-organised answer linking anatomy to clinical events.
questions.modelAnswer:
The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is formed by levator ani and coccygeus. Levator ani has three parts: puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus. Below it lies the diamond-shaped perineum, divided by a line between the ischial tuberosities into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind. The perineal body sits at the centre. Bulbospongiosus, the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, the external anal sphincter and fibres of levator ani all attach to it, so damage to it weakens perineal support.

The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. It curves around the sacrospinous ligament close to the ischial spine, re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen and runs forward in the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. It gives the inferior rectal, perineal and dorsal clitoral nerves. For a block, the ischial spine is felt through the lateral vaginal wall and local anaesthetic is injected just behind and below it, numbing most of the perineum for an instrumental delivery.

A midline episiotomy cuts towards the perineal body and anal sphincter and is more likely to extend into a third- or fourth-degree tear. A mediolateral incision, angled away from the midline, avoids the sphincter complex.

Faecal continence depends on several structures:
- The internal anal sphincter, a thickening of circular smooth muscle, provides most resting tone.
- The external anal sphincter, skeletal muscle supplied by the inferior rectal nerve, allows voluntary squeeze.
- Puborectalis loops around the anorectal junction to keep the anorectal angle.
- Rectal compliance, and the sensitive anoderm below the pectinate line, help tell gas from stool.

Childbirth can tear the sphincters directly (obstetric anal sphincter injury), sometimes without an obvious tear on the surface. A long second stage and forceps can also stretch or compress the pudendal nerve, weakening the external sphincter and puborectalis. Ms Rahman's urgency and flatus incontinence suggest external sphincter dysfunction. She should be assessed with endoanal ultrasound and anorectal physiology, and offered pelvic floor physiotherapy with specialist follow-up.

questions.q:
Liam, a 25-year-old motorcyclist, is thrown from his bike and lands on his shoulder with his head forced sharply to the left. He is brought in with his right arm hanging by his side, medially rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. He cannot abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow. There is numbness over the lateral arm and forearm. The biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are absent on the right.

Identify the injury, explain each clinical feature in terms of the nerves and muscles affected, and explain how you would distinguish it from a lower plexus (C8–T1) injury.
markScheme: Upper brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy), C5–C6 roots or upper trunk, from traction widening the angle between neck and shoulder.
Loss of abduction: deltoid (axillary nerve) and supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) weak.
Medial rotation: the lateral rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor; C5–C6) are weak, leaving pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi (substantial C7–T1 supply) relatively unopposed.
Elbow extended: biceps and brachialis (musculocutaneous) and brachioradialis (radial C5–C6) weak; triceps (C7) partly intact.
Pronated forearm: supinator and biceps (main supinator) weak.
Sensory loss: C5 lateral arm, C6 lateral forearm and thumb.
Absent biceps (C5–C6) and brachioradialis (C6) reflexes.
Lower plexus (Klumpke) injury: from forced abduction; intrinsic hand weakness, claw hand, medial forearm sensory loss (T1, C8), possibly Horner's syndrome.
Horner's syndrome in an upper lesion would suggest a more extensive or root avulsion injury.
Investigation: MRI, nerve conduction/EMG; root avulsion changes prognosis.
questions.modelAnswer:
Liam has an upper brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy) affecting the C5 and C6 roots or the upper trunk. Forcing the head away from a depressed shoulder widens the neck–shoulder angle and stretches the upper roots most.

Each feature follows from loss of C5–C6 muscles:
- No shoulder abduction: deltoid (axillary nerve) and supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) are both mainly C5–C6.
- Medial rotation: the lateral rotators, infraspinatus and teres minor (both C5–C6), are weak. Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, which draw substantially on C7–T1, are left relatively unopposed. (Subscapularis is itself mainly C5–C6, so it is weakened too.)
- Extended elbow: the elbow flexors are paralysed. These are biceps and brachialis (musculocutaneous nerve) and brachioradialis (radial nerve, C5–C6). Triceps, mainly C7, still works.
- Pronated forearm: biceps, the strongest supinator, and supinator itself are weak, so pronation dominates.
- Numbness of the lateral arm and forearm matches the C5 and C6 dermatomes, supplied through the axillary and musculocutaneous nerves.
- The biceps reflex (C5–C6) and brachioradialis reflex (C6) are lost.

A lower plexus (Klumpke) injury follows forced abduction, for example grabbing something while falling. It affects C8–T1 and the intrinsic hand muscles, causing clawing and wasting of the interossei and hypothenar muscles. Sensation is lost along the medial forearm and hand. If the T1 root is avulsed near the cord, the sympathetic outflow to the head is damaged and Horner's syndrome follows (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are spared.

Winging of the scapula or rhomboid weakness in Liam would suggest damage close to the cord (possibly root avulsion), because the long thoracic and dorsal scapular nerves leave from the roots. Horner's syndrome would mean the injury also reached T1, implying a more extensive, often avulsion, injury. MRI and nerve conduction studies with electromyography help distinguish avulsion from injury further out, which matters because avulsed roots do not recover on their own and may need nerve transfer surgery.

questions.q:
Mrs Joan Ellis, 81, falls at home and cannot stand. Her right leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the right femoral neck. During her stay a nurse gives an intramuscular injection into the buttock, after which she reports numbness of the sole of the foot and weakness of knee flexion and all foot movements.

Explain the anatomy behind the leg's position and the choice of surgical treatment for her fracture. Then identify the nerve likely to have been injured by the injection, describe the expected deficits, and explain how intramuscular gluteal injections should be given to avoid this.
markScheme: Shortening: pull of muscles crossing the fracture (gluteals, hamstrings, adductors, rectus femoris) draws the distal fragment upward.
External rotation: iliopsoas (inserting on lesser trochanter) and short lateral rotators act on the distal fragment once the neck is broken.
Femoral head blood supply mainly from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running up the neck within the capsule.
Artery of ligamentum teres (from obturator) is small and insufficient in adults.
Displaced intracapsular fracture tears retinacular vessels, so high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.
Therefore usually treated with hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement rather than fixation in the older patient.
Injection injury: sciatic nerve (L4–S3), passing below piriformis through the lower medial part of the buttock.
Deficits: weak knee flexion (hamstrings), loss of all muscles below the knee (tibial and common fibular), foot drop, sensory loss below the knee except medial leg (saphenous), absent ankle jerk.
Safe site: upper outer quadrant of the buttock, or ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius between ASIS and iliac tubercle).
Note that knee extension and hip adduction are spared (femoral and obturator nerves).
questions.modelAnswer:
In a displaced femoral neck fracture the femoral shaft is no longer held by the neck. Muscles crossing the hip pull the distal fragment upward and shorten the leg; these include the gluteals, hamstrings, adductors and rectus femoris. Iliopsoas, attached to the lesser trochanter, and the short lateral rotators acting at the greater trochanter turn the shaft outward, producing external rotation.

The adult femoral head gets most of its blood from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery. These vessels run up the back of the neck under the capsule's synovial reflection. The artery of the ligamentum teres, from the obturator artery, is small and contributes little in older adults. A displaced intracapsular fracture is likely to tear the retinacular vessels, so the head is at high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union. In an older patient this usually means replacing the head with a hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement rather than fixing it with screws, which allows early weight-bearing. Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures keep their blood supply and are usually fixed.

The injection probably damaged the sciatic nerve (L4–S3). It leaves the pelvis below piriformis and passes down through the lower, inner part of the buttock, midway between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. The expected deficits are:
- Weak knee flexion from loss of the hamstrings.
