- Paralysis of all muscles below the knee: dorsiflexors and evertors through the common fibular nerve, and plantarflexors and invertors through the tibial nerve. This produces a flail foot.
- Sensory loss over the sole, dorsum and lateral leg, with the medial leg spared because it is supplied by the saphenous nerve from the femoral nerve.
- An absent ankle jerk. Knee extension and the knee jerk (femoral) and hip adduction (obturator) are spared.

To avoid this, gluteal injections should go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, well above and lateral to the nerve's path. The ventrogluteal site, in gluteus medius within the triangle formed by the anterior superior iliac spine, iliac tubercle and greater trochanter, is preferred because it lies far from major nerves and vessels.

questions.q:
Mr Gareth Hughes, 47, wakes one morning with drooping of the right side of his face. He cannot close his right eye or wrinkle his right forehead, and food collects in his right cheek. He reports that sounds seem unpleasantly loud in his right ear and that food tastes odd on the right side of his tongue. Tear production seems reduced on the right. Hearing is otherwise normal and the rest of the neurological examination is normal.

Identify the lesion. Using the course of the facial nerve, explain each feature and how the level of the lesion can be inferred. Contrast this with the facial weakness seen after a stroke.
markScheme: Right lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, likely Bell's palsy (idiopathic), with lesion in the facial canal proximal to the geniculate ganglion region.
Course: pons, cerebellopontine angle, internal acoustic meatus with VIII, facial canal, geniculate ganglion, stylomastoid foramen, parotid.
Whole hemiface weakness including forehead = lower motor neuron.
Inability to close eye: orbicularis oculi; food in cheek: buccinator.
Hyperacusis: nerve to stapedius lost (branch in the facial canal).
Altered taste anterior two-thirds of the tongue: chorda tympani, which leaves in the facial canal above the stylomastoid foramen.
Reduced tearing: greater petrosal nerve leaves at the geniculate ganglion, so lesion at or proximal to it.
A lesion only at the stylomastoid foramen (e.g. parotid tumour) would cause only motor weakness.
Normal hearing argues against a cerebellopontine angle lesion affecting VIII.
UMN (stroke): lower face weakness only, forehead spared due to bilateral cortical input; usually with limb weakness.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Hughes has a right-sided lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy. The sudden onset and absence of other neurological signs fit Bell's palsy, an idiopathic inflammatory swelling of the nerve in the narrow facial canal.

The facial nerve leaves the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction and crosses the cerebellopontine angle with the vestibulocochlear nerve. It enters the internal acoustic meatus and runs through the facial canal in the temporal bone. At the bend called the geniculate ganglion it gives off the greater petrosal nerve, carrying secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland. Further along the canal it gives the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani, which carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. It then leaves through the stylomastoid foramen and divides in the parotid into its five motor branches.

How each feature arises:
- Weakness of the whole right side of the face, including the forehead, shows a lower motor neuron lesion. Orbicularis oculi cannot close the eye, and weakness of buccinator lets food collect in the cheek.
- Hyperacusis follows loss of stapedius, which normally damps movement of the stapes.
- Altered taste on the right of the tongue means the chorda tympani is involved.
- Reduced tearing means the greater petrosal fibres are affected, placing the lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion.

A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen, such as a parotid tumour, would cause facial weakness alone, with normal taste, tearing and stapedius function. Normal hearing makes a cerebellopontine angle mass such as a vestibular schwannoma less likely, because that would usually affect VIII as well.

After a stroke, the lesion lies in the upper motor neuron pathway. The forehead is spared because the facial motor neurons for the upper face receive input from both hemispheres. Weakness mainly affects the lower face on the side opposite the lesion and is often accompanied by arm and leg weakness on the same side as the facial weakness.

questions.q: 'The thyroid gland is the most dangerous organ in the neck for a surgeon, not because of its own structure, but because of what lies around it.' Discuss this statement with reference to the embryology, blood supply, relations and nerve supply of the thyroid and parathyroid glands, and the complications that follow thyroidectomy.
markScheme: Embryology: thyroid from endodermal diverticulum at foramen caecum, descends via thyroglossal duct; remnants cause thyroglossal cysts that move on tongue protrusion.
Parathyroids: inferior from third pouch (with thymus), superior from fourth pouch; inferior glands variable in position (may be in thymus/mediastinum).
Relations: isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4; lobes against larynx, trachea, oesophagus, carotid sheath laterally; pretracheal fascia (moves with swallowing).
Blood supply: superior thyroid artery (external carotid), inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk), occasional thyroid ima; veins superior, middle, inferior.
External laryngeal nerve runs with superior thyroid artery: ligate artery close to the gland to protect it; injury affects cricothyroid and pitch.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve in tracheo-oesophageal groove, related to inferior thyroid artery near Berry's ligament; injury causes hoarseness (unilateral) or stridor/airway obstruction (bilateral).
Parathyroid blood supply mainly from inferior thyroid artery; devascularisation or removal causes hypocalcaemia (tingling, tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau signs).
Haemorrhage under pretracheal fascia can compress the airway: neck haematoma is an emergency.
Other complications: hypothyroidism, thyroid storm (historically in poorly prepared hyperthyroid patients), wound issues.
Balanced argument: the gland itself is also relevant (vascularity, retrosternal extension, malignancy), so 'not because of its own structure' is partly overstated.
Intraoperative strategies: identify RLN, preserve parathyroids with their blood supply, nerve monitoring.
Well-structured essay with a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement captures a real surgical truth, but it understates the thyroid's own contribution to risk.

Embryology explains much of the danger. The thyroid descends from the foramen caecum along the thyroglossal duct, whose remnants form midline cysts. The superior parathyroids (pouch 4) stay fairly constant near the cricothyroid junction. The inferior pair (pouch 3) migrates with the thymus and may lie anywhere from the jaw angle to the mediastinum, making it hard to find and protect.

The gland lies within pretracheal fascia, its isthmus over tracheal rings two to four, its lobes against the larynx, trachea and oesophagus, with the carotid sheath laterally. It is supplied by the superior thyroid artery (external carotid) and inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk). Bleeding inside the closed fascial space can compress the airway, so a tense postoperative haematoma must be opened at once.

The nerves at risk:
- The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery. Tying the artery close to the gland protects it. Injury paralyses cricothyroid, causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue, which matters especially to singers.
- The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and is closely related to branches of the inferior thyroid artery and to the posterior suspensory (Berry's) ligament. Damage to one nerve causes hoarseness. Damage to both can leave the vocal folds near the midline, causing stridor and airway obstruction.

The parathyroids get most of their blood from the inferior thyroid artery. Removing them or cutting off their blood supply causes hypocalcaemia, with perioral tingling, tetany and Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs. This is the most common significant complication of total thyroidectomy and is often temporary.

The gland's own features matter too: retrosternal goitres, vascular Graves' glands and invasive cancers make surgery harder, and hypothyroidism follows total removal.

In conclusion, most serious complications do come from neighbouring structures whose positions follow from development. Careful identification of them, often with nerve monitoring, is the core of safe thyroid surgery.

questions.q:
Baby Noah is born at term. At birth, a midline defect at the umbilicus is seen, through which loops of bowel and part of the liver protrude, covered by a thin translucent membrane into which the umbilical cord inserts. Later in childhood a different child, Ella, aged 2, presents with painless rectal bleeding and is found to have a diverticulum on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.

Using the embryology of the midgut, explain both conditions. Include in your answer the normal process of physiological herniation and rotation, and compare Noah's condition with gastroschisis.
markScheme: Midgut supplied by SMA; elongates rapidly and herniates into the umbilical cord in week 6 (physiological herniation) because the abdomen is too small.
Rotates 270° anticlockwise (viewed from front) around SMA axis: 90° during herniation, 180° on return.
Returns to the abdomen at weeks 10–12; caecum descends to right iliac fossa.
Omphalocele: failure of the midgut to return; contents covered by amnion/peritoneum sac, cord inserts into sac.
Omphalocele often associated with other anomalies (chromosomal e.g. trisomy 18/13, cardiac, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome).
Gastroschisis: full-thickness abdominal wall defect, usually right of the umbilicus, no covering sac, cord separate; rarely associated with chromosomal anomalies; bowel exposed to amniotic fluid.
Vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and normally obliterates early, around weeks 5–7.
Meckel's diverticulum: persistent proximal vitelline duct on antimesenteric border of ileum.
May contain ectopic gastric (or pancreatic) mucosa; acid ulcerates adjacent ileum, causing painless bleeding.
Other complications: intussusception, volvulus, diverticulitis mimicking appendicitis.
Malrotation as another midgut rotation error causing volvulus (bonus).
questions.modelAnswer:
The midgut runs from the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the transverse colon and is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. In week 6 it lengthens faster than the abdomen can hold, and the liver and kidneys take up much of the space. A loop of midgut therefore herniates into the umbilical cord. This is physiological herniation. Its apex stays connected to the yolk sac by the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, and the superior mesenteric artery runs down its centre as the axis.

While herniated, the loop rotates 90° anticlockwise, viewed from the front. When it returns at weeks 10–12, it rotates a further 180°, making 270° in total. This brings the small bowel back first and leaves the caecum high on the right, from where it later descends to the right iliac fossa. Errors in rotation cause malrotation, with a narrow mesenteric base that can twist into a midgut volvulus.

Noah has an omphalocele (exomphalos), meaning the herniated gut failed to return. The contents sit in a sac of amnion and peritoneum, the cord inserts into the sac, and liver may be included. Omphaloceles are often linked with other anomalies, including trisomies 13 and 18, heart defects and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, so these should be looked for.

Gastroschisis is a full-thickness wall defect, usually right of a normally inserted cord, with no sac; the exposed bowel may be thickened and inflamed. It is usually isolated.

Ella has a Meckel's diverticulum. The vitelline duct normally disappears early in development. If its intestinal end persists, it forms a true diverticulum on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, usually within about 60 cm of the ileocaecal valve. It may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. Acid from gastric mucosa ulcerates the neighbouring ileum, causing painless rectal bleeding in young children. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan detects the gastric mucosa. Other complications include intussusception, volvulus around a fibrous band to the umbilicus, and diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis.

questions.q: 'Understanding the pharyngeal apparatus is the key to understanding the anatomy of the adult head and neck.' Critically evaluate this proposition, using examples from the skeletal, muscular, nervous and vascular derivatives of the pharyngeal arches and pouches, and from congenital anomalies.
markScheme: Overview: arches of mesoderm and neural crest, with ectodermal clefts outside and endodermal pouches inside; each arch has cartilage, muscle, nerve and artery.
Arch 1 (V3): mastication muscles, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini; malleus, incus, Meckel's cartilage.
Arch 2 (VII): facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric; stapes, styloid, lesser horn of hyoid.

Arch 3 (IX): stylopharyngeus; greater horn of hyoid. Arches 4 and 6 (X): pharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid (superior laryngeal), intrinsic laryngeal muscles (recurrent laryngeal); laryngeal cartilages.
Explains nerve supply patterns that otherwise seem random (e.g. digastric has two nerves; tensor tympani vs stapedius).
Pouches: 1 middle ear/auditory tube, 2 palatine tonsil, 3 inferior parathyroid/thymus, 4 superior parathyroid and ultimopharyngeal body.
Arteries: 3rd carotids, 4th aortic arch (L)/right subclavian, 6th pulmonary arteries/ductus — explains recurrent laryngeal asymmetry.
Anomalies: branchial cleft cysts/fistulae (anterior to SCM), DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2: thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, cardiac outflow defects), Treacher Collins (first arch).

Limitations: much head and neck anatomy is not arch-derived — e.g. tongue muscles from occipital somites (XII), extraocular muscles (III, IV, VI), neurocranium, thyroid from floor of pharynx, cranial nerves I and II.
Arch-based rules have exceptions (e.g. tongue sensation shift, palatoglossus).
Conclusion: a strong organising principle for branchial structures but not a complete key.
Quality of critical evaluation and structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
The pharyngeal apparatus is a powerful organising idea, but calling it 'the key' to the whole head and neck overstates its reach.

From week 4, arches form on the side of the pharynx, with ectodermal clefts outside and endodermal pouches inside. Each arch has its own cartilage, muscles, nerve and artery, and these links persist, explaining patterns that otherwise look arbitrary:
- First arch (V3): muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, plus the malleus and incus.
- Second arch (VII): muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric, plus the stapes and styloid process. This is why digastric has two nerves and why the two muscles of the middle ear are supplied by different nerves.
- Third arch (IX): stylopharyngeus.
- Fourth and sixth arches (X): pharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid (superior laryngeal nerve), the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (recurrent laryngeal nerve) and the laryngeal cartilages.

The pouches give the middle ear (1), tonsillar fossa (2), inferior parathyroids and thymus (3) and superior parathyroids (4). The arch arteries explain why the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch and the right under the subclavian.

Anomalies support the case: branchial cysts along the front of sternocleidomastoid, Treacher Collins syndrome (first arch), and 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome combining thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia with outflow tract heart defects.

Much of the head and neck is not arch-derived, however. Tongue muscles come from occipital somites (XII), and extraocular muscles from head mesoderm (III, IV, VI). The cranial vault, eye and olfactory system have separate origins, and the thyroid comes from the pharyngeal floor. The rules also have exceptions, such as palatoglossus (X).

The pharyngeal apparatus is therefore the key to the branchial parts of the head and neck, but it is one essential framework among several, not a complete explanation.

questions.q:
Mr Kwame Asante, 23, is stabbed in the left side of the chest during a fight. He arrives breathless, with a respiratory rate of 32/min, oxygen saturation of 88% on air and a heart rate of 128/min. The trachea is deviated to the right, the left hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and his neck veins are distended. His blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. A wound is seen in the left fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Explain the anatomy behind his signs. Describe where and how you would decompress the chest and then insert a chest drain, naming the layers traversed and the structures at risk, and explain why the drain is passed over the upper border of the rib.
markScheme: Tension pneumothorax: one-way valve lets air into the pleural space on inspiration but not out.
Rising intrapleural pressure collapses the left lung and pushes the mediastinum (and trachea) to the right.
Mediastinal shift and raised intrathoracic pressure kink and compress the great veins, reducing venous return: distended neck veins, hypotension, tachycardia.
Hyperresonance and absent breath sounds: air in the pleural space, lung collapsed away from the chest wall.

Immediate decompression (needle or finger thoracostomy), with the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line now favoured in adults over the second space midclavicular line.
Definitive chest drain in the triangle of safety: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, line at the fifth intercostal space, apex below the axilla.
Layers: skin, subcutaneous fat, serratus anterior, external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles, endothoracic fascia, parietal pleura.
Neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs in the costal groove under the rib above, between internal and innermost intercostals: so go over the upper border of the rib below.
Structures at risk: long thoracic nerve (behind, on serratus anterior), intercostal vessels, and below the fifth space the diaphragm, spleen or liver; in front, internal thoracic vessels.
Blunt dissection and a finger sweep confirm entry into the pleura before passing the tube; trocars are avoided.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Asante has a left tension pneumothorax. The stab wound has created a one-way valve: air enters the pleural space on each breath but cannot leave. Intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric, the left lung collapses, and the mediastinum is pushed to the right, deviating the trachea. The raised pressure and mediastinal shift compress and kink the venae cavae, reducing venous return, so the neck veins distend and cardiac output falls, causing hypotension and tachycardia. Air between the chest wall and the collapsed lung gives a hyperresonant percussion note and absent breath sounds. This is a clinical diagnosis and needs treating before imaging.

Immediate decompression is by needle or finger thoracostomy. In adults the fourth or fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line is now generally preferred to the second space in the midclavicular line, because the chest wall there is thinner and a needle is more likely to reach the pleura.

A chest drain then goes in through the triangle of safety. This is bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a line level with the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla. After local anaesthesia, an incision is made and blunt dissection passes through subcutaneous fat, serratus anterior, the external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles, the endothoracic fascia and the parietal pleura. A finger sweep confirms the pleural space before the tube is passed, and a sharp trocar is avoided.

The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove on the lower border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Passing just over the upper border of the rib below avoids the main bundle. Other structures at risk are the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior behind the triangle, the internal thoracic vessels in front, and the diaphragm, spleen or liver if the drain is placed too low. The intercostal nerve is also the source of pain at the drain site, which is why the periosteum and pleura are generously anaesthetised.

questions.q:
Mrs Rosa Ferreira, 52, has had recurrent biliary colic and one episode of acute cholecystitis. She undergoes an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The operation is difficult because of dense inflammatory adhesions around the gallbladder neck. The surgeon notes a short cystic duct and an artery passing in front of the common hepatic duct, and clips and divides the structures she believes to be the cystic duct and artery. She is discharged the next day, but on day 3 she returns with jaundice, pale stools, dark urine and mild upper abdominal discomfort.

Discuss the surgical anatomy of the biliary tree and its blood supply, including common variations. Explain how the 'critical view of safety' reduces the risk of bile duct injury, why this patient's jaundice may have occurred, and the vascular consequences of injury to nearby arteries.
markScheme: Biliary tree: right and left hepatic ducts form common hepatic duct; cystic duct joins to form the common bile duct; CBD passes behind the duodenum, through pancreas head, joins pancreatic duct at the ampulla (sphincter of Oddi).
Calot's triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior surface of the liver; contains the cystic artery and often a lymph node (Lund's/Mascagni's).
Cystic artery usually from right hepatic artery; variations include origin from left hepatic, common hepatic or gastroduodenal, passing anterior to the CHD; double cystic arteries.
Right hepatic artery may arise from the SMA (replaced) and run behind the portal vein/to the right of CBD.
Duct variations: short or absent cystic duct, low insertion, aberrant right sectoral ducts draining into cystic duct or CHD.
Critical view of safety: clear Calot's triangle of fat, separate lower gallbladder from cystic plate, only two structures seen entering the gallbladder before clipping.
Classic injury: mistaking CBD for cystic duct, especially with traction aligning them; or clip encroaching on CHD with a short cystic duct.
Jaundice with pale stools and dark urine = obstructive (conjugated) jaundice; suggests clipped/transected CBD/CHD or retained stone.
Investigation: LFTs, ultrasound, MRCP/ERCP.
Bile duct blood supply mainly axial (3 o'clock and 9 o'clock arteries) from below (gastroduodenal/posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal) and above (right hepatic): ischaemia causes stricture.
Right hepatic artery injury: ischaemic biliary stricture, sometimes liver infarction/abscess.
Depth, accurate terminology and logical structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct, which the cystic duct joins to form the common bile duct. This runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, behind the first part of the duodenum and through the pancreatic head, usually joining the pancreatic duct at the ampulla (sphincter of Oddi).

The hepatocystic (Calot's) triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and inferior liver surface. It usually contains the cystic artery, from the right hepatic artery, and the cystic node. Variations underlie many injuries:
- The cystic artery may arise from the left hepatic, common hepatic or gastroduodenal artery and cross in front of the common hepatic duct, as here, or be double.
- A replaced right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery runs right of the bile duct; the right hepatic artery may loop close to the cystic duct and be mistaken for the cystic artery.
- The cystic duct may be short, run parallel or join low; aberrant right sectoral ducts may drain into it.

Strasberg's critical view of safety requires, before clipping, a triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder lifted off the cystic plate, and only two structures seen entering the gallbladder. This prevents the classic error in which traction aligns the common bile duct with the cystic duct and the common duct is clipped and divided.

Mrs Ferreira's jaundice is obstructive. A retained stone is possible, but a short cystic duct and difficult dissection raise the possibility of a clipped or narrowed common duct. She needs liver function tests, ultrasound for dilated ducts or a collection, and MRCP or ERCP.

The bile duct is supplied by fine axial arteries at 3 and 9 o'clock, mostly from below (gastroduodenal and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal) and partly from the right hepatic artery. Stripping the duct or injuring the right hepatic artery can cause ischaemic strictures weeks or months later, and severe arterial injury can cause right liver ischaemia or abscess, complicating repair.
